notes.front: In CKA, what does etcdctl snapshot save do and what env vars does it need?
notes.back: Takes a point-in-time backup of the etcd datastore (the cluster's source of truth). You must set ETCDCTL_API=3 and pass --endpoints, --cacert, --cert, and --key (the etcd server CA and client certs). Restore with etcdctl snapshot restore into a new data dir, then point the static pod manifest at it.

notes.front: What is the correct order to upgrade a kubeadm cluster?
notes.back: 1) Upgrade kubeadm on the control-plane node; 2) kubeadm upgrade plan then kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z; 3) upgrade kubelet + kubectl on that node and restart kubelet; 4) for each worker: kubeadm upgrade node, then drain, upgrade kubelet/kubectl, uncordon. Upgrade one minor version at a time.

notes.front: Before upgrading or doing maintenance on a node, what two kubectl commands isolate it and restore it?
notes.back: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data cordons the node and evicts pods (respecting PodDisruptionBudgets). After maintenance, kubectl uncordon <node> makes it schedulable again. kubectl cordon alone only marks unschedulable without evicting.

notes.front: What are the four RBAC objects and how do they pair?
notes.back: Role-Based Access Control: Role (namespaced permissions) bound by RoleBinding; ClusterRole (cluster-wide or reusable permissions) bound by ClusterRoleBinding. A RoleBinding can also reference a ClusterRole to grant its rules within a single namespace. Rules are purely additive — there are no deny rules.

notes.front: How do you test whether a subject is allowed to perform an action?
notes.back: kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as <user> -n <ns>. Example: kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as dev -n web. Use --list to enumerate all permissions for a subject.

notes.front: What is a static pod and how does the kubelet find it?
notes.back: A pod managed directly by the kubelet on a node (not the API server / scheduler). The kubelet watches the directory in --pod-manifest-path (default /etc/kubernetes/manifests) and runs any pod manifest placed there. Control-plane components (apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) run as static pods in kubeadm clusters. A read-only mirror pod appears in the API.

notes.front: What is the difference between a taint and a toleration?
notes.back: A taint is placed on a node (kubectl taint nodes n key=val:NoSchedule) to repel pods. A toleration is placed on a pod to allow (not require) scheduling onto a tainted node. Taint effects: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute (also evicts running pods that don't tolerate).

notes.front: Node affinity vs pod affinity vs pod anti-affinity?
notes.back: Node affinity: attract a pod to nodes by node labels. Pod affinity: co-locate a pod near other pods (by their labels) in a topology domain. Pod anti-affinity: keep pods apart (e.g. spread replicas across zones). Each is requiredDuringScheduling... (hard) or preferred... (soft).

notes.front: What do the PersistentVolume reclaim policies Retain, Delete, and Recycle mean?
notes.back: Govern what happens to a PersistentVolume after its claim is deleted. Retain: keep the volume + data, manual cleanup. Delete: delete the underlying storage asset. Recycle: deprecated (scrubbed and reused). Dynamically provisioned volumes default to Delete via the StorageClass.

notes.front: What does a StorageClass provide, and what is WaitForFirstConsumer?
notes.back: A StorageClass defines a provisioner + parameters for dynamic volume provisioning. volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer delays binding/provisioning until a pod using the claim is scheduled, so the volume lands in the right zone/topology (avoids zone mismatch). The alternative is Immediate.

notes.front: In CKA cluster networking, what must every CNI plugin guarantee?
notes.back: The Container Network Interface model requires: every pod gets its own IP; pods on any node can reach pods on any other node without NAT; and a node's agents (kubelet) can reach all pods on that node. The pod CIDR must not overlap node/service CIDRs.

notes.front: What provides in-cluster DNS and what is a Service's DNS name?
notes.back: CoreDNS (running as a Deployment, exposed by the kube-dns Service). A Service resolves at <svc>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Pods get DNS config via the kubelet pointing /etc/resolv.conf at the cluster DNS ClusterIP.

notes.front: What are the kube-proxy modes and the modern default direction?
notes.back: kube-proxy implements Service virtual IPs. Modes: iptables (default historically), ipvs (better at scale, hash-based LB), and userspace (legacy). Newer dataplanes (e.g. Cilium) can replace kube-proxy entirely using eBPF.

notes.front: How long are kubeadm certificates valid and how do you check/renew?
notes.back: Client/serving certs default to 1 year; the cluster CA to 10 years. Check with kubeadm certs check-expiration; renew all with kubeadm certs renew all (renewed automatically on control-plane upgrade).

notes.front: A pod is stuck in Pending. What is your first triage command and common causes?
notes.back: kubectl describe pod and read Events. Common Pending causes: insufficient CPU/memory on nodes, unsatisfied nodeSelector/affinity/taints, unbound PVC, or no nodes Ready. kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp gives cluster-wide context.

notes.front: If the API server is down in a kubeadm cluster, where do you look?
notes.back: It runs as a static pod, so kubectl won't work. Check kubelet: journalctl -u kubelet, the container runtime (crictl ps, crictl logs), and the manifest /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Verify etcd is healthy and certs/flags are valid.

notes.front: What is the difference between requests and limits, and what is the QoS impact?
notes.back: requests = guaranteed/scheduled amount; limits = hard ceiling. QoS classes: Guaranteed (requests==limits for all resources), Burstable (some requests set), BestEffort (none set). Under node memory pressure, BestEffort pods are evicted first, then Burstable. CPU over-limit is throttled; memory over-limit is OOM-killed.

notes.front: What does a ResourceQuota vs a LimitRange control?
notes.back: ResourceQuota: aggregate caps per namespace (total CPU/memory/object counts). LimitRange: per-object defaults and min/max (e.g. default container requests, max PVC size). LimitRange auto-fills requests/limits when pods omit them.

notes.front: What is the role of kubeconfig contexts and how do you switch?
notes.back: A kubeconfig bundles clusters, users, and contexts (a cluster+user+namespace tuple). kubectl config get-contexts, kubectl config use-context <name>, kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns>. The active context is the default target for commands.

notes.front: How do you generate a YAML manifest fast in the exam without writing it by hand?
notes.back: Use --dry-run=client -o yaml. Example: kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > d.yaml. kubectl run, create job/cronjob/configmap/secret/role all support this for scaffolding.

notes.front: What is the difference between a DaemonSet and a Deployment for placement?
notes.back: A DaemonSet runs exactly one pod per (matching) node and auto-adds pods to new nodes — used for node agents (CNI, log/metrics collectors). A Deployment runs N replicas placed by the scheduler anywhere. DaemonSet pods tolerate node taints by default for system roles.

notes.front: What is a CertificateSigningRequest (CSR) used for in cluster admin?
notes.back: To issue a client cert for a new user. Submit a base64 CSR as a CertificateSigningRequest object, kubectl certificate approve <csr>, then extract the signed cert and build a kubeconfig. RBAC then authorizes that user/CN.

notes.front: What information does kubectl top need and provide?
notes.back: Live CPU/memory usage for nodes and pods. Requires the metrics-server add-on (aggregated API metrics.k8s.io). Not historical — for that use Prometheus. kubectl top nodes, kubectl top pods -n ns.

notes.front: What is the Gateway API and how does it differ from Ingress?
notes.back: A newer, role-oriented, more expressive successor to Ingress for L4/L7 routing. Splits responsibilities across GatewayClass (infra), Gateway (a listener/instance), and HTTPRoute/TCPRoute (routing rules). More portable and extensible than the single overloaded Ingress object; CRDs are installed separately.

notes.front: What are the 4Cs of Cloud Native Security?
notes.back: Nested layers, secured outside-in: Cloud (or datacenter infra) → Cluster (Kubernetes components, RBAC, network policy) → Container (image hygiene, runtime) → Code (app security, TLS, deps). A weak outer layer can't be saved by a strong inner one.

notes.front: What is a default-deny NetworkPolicy and why start there?
notes.back: A NetworkPolicy selecting all pods with empty ingress (and/or egress) blocks all traffic to/from them; you then add explicit allow rules. Pods are non-isolated by default (all traffic allowed), so default-deny establishes least-privilege networking. Requires a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy (e.g. Calico, Cilium).
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · network policy

notes.front: What are the three Pod Security Standards profiles?
notes.back: Privileged (unrestricted), Baseline (blocks known privilege escalations; minimally restrictive), Restricted (hardened best practice: non-root, drop capabilities, seccomp RuntimeDefault, no host namespaces). Enforced by Pod Security Admission via namespace labels.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · pod security

notes.front: How is Pod Security Admission configured per namespace?
notes.back: Label the namespace: pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>: <level>, where mode is enforce, audit, or warn and level is privileged/baseline/restricted. e.g. pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted. PSA is the built-in replacement for the removed PodSecurityPolicy.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · pod security

notes.front: What is seccomp and how do you enable the default profile on a pod?
notes.back: Secure Computing mode filters which syscalls a container may make. Set securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault (the container runtime's curated profile) or Localhost with a custom profile path. Blocks dangerous syscalls to shrink the kernel attack surface.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · runtime hardening

notes.front: What does AppArmor do for containers and how is it applied now?
notes.back: A Linux Mandatory Access Control module restricting a process's file/capability/network access via a per-profile policy. In recent Kubernetes it's set via the pod/container securityContext.appArmorProfile field (older clusters used the container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container> annotation).
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · runtime hardening

notes.front: Which Linux capabilities should you drop, and how?
notes.back: Drop all then add only what's needed: securityContext.capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"], add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]}. Avoid CAP_SYS_ADMIN and privileged mode. Combine with runAsNonRoot: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, and a read-only root filesystem.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · runtime hardening

notes.front: What is Falco and what does it detect?
notes.back: A CNCF runtime-security tool that taps kernel syscalls (eBPF or a kernel module) and alerts on suspicious behavior at runtime — e.g. a shell spawned in a container, writes to /etc, unexpected outbound connections, or reads of sensitive files. Rules are YAML; it complements (not replaces) admission-time controls.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · runtime security

notes.front: What is kube-bench and what does it check?
notes.back: A tool that runs the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Kubernetes Benchmark against a cluster, checking control-plane flags, file permissions, and worker configs for hardening compliance, and reporting pass/fail/remediation.

notes.front: What is Trivy used for in a CKS context?
notes.back: An open-source scanner for container images, filesystems, and IaC. Finds OS/library CVEs (vulnerabilities), misconfigurations, secrets, and can generate an SBOM. Typically run in CI to gate images before they reach a registry/cluster.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · supply chain

notes.front: What is image signing with Cosign and why does it matter?
notes.back: Cosign (Sigstore project) cryptographically signs container images; the signature is stored in the registry. Admission policies (Kyverno verifyImages, or a policy controller) verify the signature before allowing deployment — ensuring image provenance/integrity in the software supply chain. Supports keyless (OIDC) signing.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · supply chain

notes.front: What is an SBOM and why generate one?
notes.back: Software Bill of Materials: a machine-readable inventory of all components/dependencies in an artifact (formats: SPDX, CycloneDX). Enables fast impact analysis when a new CVE drops (e.g. Log4Shell) and is increasingly required for supply-chain compliance.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · supply chain

notes.front: How do you encrypt Kubernetes Secrets at rest in etcd?
notes.back: Configure an EncryptionConfiguration on the API server (--encryption-provider-config) with a provider such as aescbc/aesgcm or a KMS plugin. By default Secrets are only base64-encoded in etcd, not encrypted. After enabling, re-encrypt existing secrets with kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -.

notes.front: What is the API server audit policy and its levels?
notes.back: The audit policy defines what API requests are logged. Levels per rule: None, Metadata (request metadata only), Request (+ request body), RequestResponse (+ response body). Configured via --audit-policy-file and --audit-log-path. Critical for incident forensics.

notes.front: Why disable automatic ServiceAccount token mounting where unused?
notes.back: A mounted SA token can be exfiltrated and used against the API server. Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the pod or ServiceAccount when the workload doesn't call the API. Modern tokens are short-lived, audience-bound projected tokens rather than long-lived secrets.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · least privilege

notes.front: What are admission controllers and the two webhook types?
notes.back: Plugins in the API request path that intercept create/update before persistence. MutatingAdmissionWebhook can modify objects; ValidatingAdmissionWebhook can accept/reject. Mutating runs before validating. Tools like Kyverno/Gatekeeper register as webhooks; ImagePolicyWebhook gates images.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · admission control

notes.front: What does the ImagePolicyWebhook admission controller do?
notes.back: Sends each pod's images to an external service that returns allow/deny, letting you enforce image provenance/scan policy at admission. Enabled via the API server --admission-control-config-file; failing open vs closed is configurable.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · admission control

notes.front: What is gVisor / Kata Containers and when use them?
notes.back: Stronger workload isolation via a sandboxed runtime: gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel; Kata runs each pod in a lightweight VM. Selected per-pod via a RuntimeClass. Use for untrusted/multi-tenant workloads where namespace isolation is insufficient.

notes.front: What is a RuntimeClass?
notes.back: A cluster resource selecting which container runtime handler runs a pod (e.g. runc, gvisor, kata). Set spec.runtimeClassName on the pod. Enables mixing standard and sandboxed runtimes on the same cluster.

notes.front: How do you minimize a container image's attack surface?
notes.back: Use minimal/distroless or scratch base images, pin to digests not latest, run as non-root, drop capabilities, read-only root FS, multi-stage builds to exclude build tools, no embedded secrets, and scan in CI. Fewer binaries = fewer CVEs and no shell for an attacker.

notes.front: What is the principle behind restricting the kubelet API in hardening?
notes.back: The kubelet's read/write API (port 10250) can exec into pods and read logs. Harden by requiring authn (--anonymous-auth=false), authz mode Webhook (not AlwaysAllow), and NodeRestriction admission so a node can only modify its own objects — limiting blast radius of a compromised node.
notes.source: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist · cluster hardening

notes.front: What is OPA Gatekeeper and how does its policy model work?
notes.back: Open Policy Agent Gatekeeper is a validating admission controller using Rego policies. You define a ConstraintTemplate (the rego logic + a CRD), then create Constraints (instances binding it to resource kinds with parameters). It also supports audit of existing resources. Contrast: Kyverno uses YAML, no Rego.

notes.front: What is the CNCF and what are its project maturity levels?
notes.back: The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (under the Linux Foundation) hosts cloud-native open-source projects. Maturity: Sandbox (early) → Incubating (growing adoption) → Graduated (mature, e.g. Kubernetes, Prometheus, Envoy).

notes.front: Define cloud native (CNCF definition, in essence).
notes.back: Building/running scalable apps in modern dynamic environments using containers, microservices, immutable infrastructure, and declarative APIs, enabling loosely coupled, resilient, observable systems that allow frequent, low-risk changes.

notes.front: What are CRI, CNI, and CSI?
notes.back: Pluggable Kubernetes interfaces: Container Runtime Interface (how kubelet talks to runtimes like containerd/CRI-O), Container Network Interface (pod networking plugins), Container Storage Interface (storage drivers). Standard interfaces decouple Kubernetes from specific implementations.

notes.front: What is the OCI and its main specs?
notes.back: The Open Container Initiative standardizes container formats: the image-spec (image layout), runtime-spec (how to run a filesystem bundle), and distribution-spec (registry API). Ensures images/runtimes interoperate across tools.

notes.front: Name the three autoscalers and what each scales.
notes.back: HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler): adds/removes pod replicas on metrics. VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler): tunes pod CPU/memory requests. Cluster Autoscaler: adds/removes nodes when pods can't schedule or nodes are idle. KEDA adds event-driven scaling (to/from zero).

notes.front: What are the three pillars of observability?
notes.back: Metrics (aggregatable numeric time series, e.g. Prometheus), Logs (discrete timestamped events), and Traces (request flow across services). Often a fourth — events/profiles — is added. OpenTelemetry standardizes their collection.

notes.front: What is serverless / Knative in cloud native?
notes.back: A model where you run code without managing servers and scale to zero when idle. Knative brings serverless to Kubernetes: Serving (request-driven autoscaling incl. scale-to-zero) and Eventing (event delivery/sources/brokers).

notes.front: What is a service mesh, conceptually?
notes.back: A dedicated infrastructure layer (proxies + control plane) handling service-to-service traffic management, mutual TLS, and observability transparently to the app. Examples: Istio, Linkerd, Cilium. Moves cross-cutting networking concerns out of application code.

notes.front: What is the difference between imperative and declarative management?
notes.back: Imperative: you issue commands describing how (e.g. kubectl create, scripts). Declarative: you describe the desired end state (YAML manifests) and a controller continuously reconciles actual toward it. Kubernetes and GitOps are declarative.

notes.front: What is the reconciliation loop / controller pattern?
notes.back: Controllers continuously compare desired state (spec) with observed state (status) and take actions to converge them. This control-loop pattern is the heart of Kubernetes and underlies operators and GitOps.

notes.front: What is Helm and what is a chart?
notes.back: Helm is the Kubernetes package manager. A chart is a templated, versioned bundle of manifests; values.yaml parameterizes it; installing creates a release. Enables reuse, upgrades, and rollbacks of app deployments.

notes.front: What is the Twelve-Factor App methodology (gist)?
notes.back: A set of principles for cloud-native apps: e.g. config in the environment, stateless processes, treat backing services as attached resources, build/release/run separation, disposability, logs as event streams. Promotes portability and scalability.

notes.front: What is an Operator in Kubernetes?
notes.back: A pattern that encodes operational knowledge for a specific application as a custom controller + Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs). It automates day-2 ops (backups, upgrades, failover) by reconciling a CRD to manage the app like a human operator would.

notes.front: What is a CRD?
notes.back: A Custom Resource Definition extends the Kubernetes API with new resource types. Once registered, custom resources are managed with kubectl like built-ins and watched by custom controllers/operators. The primary extension mechanism in cloud native.

notes.front: What are the main Kubernetes Service types?
notes.back: ClusterIP (internal virtual IP, default), NodePort (exposes on a port on every node), LoadBalancer (provisions an external LB), and ExternalName (CNAME alias). Headless (clusterIP: None) returns pod IPs directly for stateful discovery.

notes.front: What roles do containerd and CRI-O play?
notes.back: They are CRI-compliant container runtimes the kubelet drives to pull images and run containers. Docker is no longer used directly by the kubelet (dockershim removed); containerd is the common default. runc is the low-level OCI runtime underneath.

notes.front: What is GitOps in one sentence (KCNA level)?
notes.back: An operating model where Git is the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure/apps, and an agent continuously reconciles the cluster to match Git, so deployments are versioned, auditable, and self-healing.

notes.front: What is the Kubernetes threat model framework often referenced (the 4As / STRIDE)?
notes.back: KCSA leans on STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. You map each Kubernetes component/trust boundary to these threats to reason about controls.
notes.source: Kubernetes & Cloud Security Associate · threat modeling

notes.front: What are the main trust boundaries in a Kubernetes cluster?
notes.back: Between: external users ↔ API server; API server ↔ etcd; control plane ↔ nodes (kubelet); node ↔ pod/container; pod ↔ pod (network); and cluster ↔ cloud/infra. Each boundary needs authn, authz, encryption, and isolation controls.

notes.front: What is the principle of "secure defaults" tension in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Many Kubernetes defaults favor usability over security (all pod traffic allowed, SA tokens auto-mounted, no Pod Security restrictions, secrets only base64). KCSA expects you to know the insecure defaults and the hardening that closes them.

notes.front: What are the four phases of the request path the API server enforces?
notes.back: Every API request goes through Authentication (who are you) → Authorization (are you allowed, via RBAC/Node/Webhook) → Admission Control (mutate/validate/policy) → persistence to etcd. KCSA tests understanding of controls at each stage.
notes.source: Kubernetes & Cloud Security Associate · API security

notes.front: What supply-chain risks does KCSA emphasize?
notes.back: Compromised base images, malicious/typosquatted dependencies, unsigned artifacts, leaked credentials, and build-system tampering. Mitigations: SBOMs, image signing (Cosign), provenance (SLSA), scanning, and admission verification.
notes.source: Kubernetes & Cloud Security Associate · supply chain

notes.front: What is SLSA?
notes.back: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: a framework of graded requirements (levels) for build integrity and provenance, hardening the path from source to artifact against tampering. Referenced for supply-chain assurance.
notes.source: Kubernetes & Cloud Security Associate · supply chain

notes.front: In KCSA, why is etcd a top-priority asset to protect?
notes.back: etcd holds all cluster state including Secrets (only base64 by default). Read access ≈ full cluster compromise. Controls: mutual TLS for etcd peers/clients, restrict to control-plane network, encryption at rest, and regular backups.

notes.front: What is the difference between authentication and authorization mechanisms in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Authn: client certs, bearer/SA tokens, OIDC, webhook — Kubernetes has no user objects. Authz: RBAC (common), ABAC, Node authorizer, and Webhook. Both must pass before admission.
notes.source: Kubernetes & Cloud Security Associate · access control

notes.front: What is microsegmentation and why apply it?
notes.back: Restricting pod-to-pod traffic to only what's required, using NetworkPolicies (or mesh authz). Limits lateral movement after a single pod is compromised — a core defense-in-depth principle for the cluster layer.
notes.source: Kubernetes & Cloud Security Associate · network security

notes.front: What categories of controls reduce container-layer risk?
notes.back: Run as non-root, drop capabilities, read-only FS, seccomp/AppArmor, no privileged mode, resource limits (DoS), trusted/scanned images, and sandboxed runtimes for untrusted workloads. Maps to the Container "C" of the 4Cs.
notes.source: Kubernetes & Cloud Security Associate · container security

notes.front: Why is observability part of security posture?
notes.back: Audit logs, runtime detection (Falco), and metrics provide the detection/response capability — you cannot respond to what you cannot see. KCSA frames logging/monitoring as a security control, not just ops.

notes.front: What is the shared responsibility model in managed Kubernetes?
notes.back: The cloud provider secures the control plane/infrastructure (the Cloud C); you secure workloads, RBAC, network policy, images, and configs (Cluster/Container/Code). Misunderstanding the split is a common gap KCSA highlights.

notes.front: What do the Linux file permission bits and chmod numeric form mean?
notes.back: Three triads — owner/group/other — each with read(4)/write(2)/execute(1). chmod 750 f = rwx for owner, r-x for group, none for other. chmod u+x f is the symbolic form. chown user:group f sets ownership.

notes.front: What are SUID, SGID, and the sticky bit?
notes.back: SUID (4xxx): run executable as the file owner. SGID (2xxx): run as the group / new files inherit dir group. Sticky bit (1xxx) on a dir: only the file owner can delete their files (e.g. /tmp). Shown as s/t in ls -l.

notes.front: How do you manage a service with systemd?
notes.back: systemctl start|stop|restart|status|enable|disable <unit>. enable sets it to start at boot; start only affects now. Unit files live in /etc/systemd/system/; after editing run systemctl daemon-reload.

notes.front: How do you read logs with journald?
notes.back: journalctl -u <unit> for a service, -f to follow, -b for current boot, --since "10 min ago", -p err by priority. Persistent storage needs /var/log/journal to exist.

notes.front: What is the modern way to inspect IP addressing and routes?
notes.back: The ip suite (iproute2): ip addr (interfaces/IPs), ip route (routing table), ip link set dev eth0 up. ss -tulpn shows listening sockets (replaces netstat).

notes.front: What is the LVM stack and its three layers?
notes.back: Logical Volume Manager: Physical Volumes (PVs, raw disks/partitions) → grouped into a Volume Group (VG) → carved into Logical Volumes (LVs) you format/mount. Enables flexible resizing: lvextend + resize2fs/xfs_growfs.

notes.front: How do you make a mount persistent across reboots?
notes.back: Add an entry to /etc/fstab: <device-or-UUID> <mountpoint> <fstype> <opts> 0 0. Use UUIDs (from blkid) over device names. Test with mount -a before rebooting to catch errors.

notes.front: How do you find and kill a process?
notes.back: Find: ps aux | grep, pgrep -f name, top/htop. Kill: kill <pid> (SIGTERM 15, graceful), kill -9 (SIGKILL, forced), pkill name. nice/renice adjust scheduling priority.

notes.front: What is the cron syntax for scheduling?
notes.back: Five fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week then the command. e.g. 0 2 * * 1 = 02:00 every Monday. User crontabs via crontab -e; system jobs in /etc/cron.d. systemd timers are the modern alternative.

notes.front: Contrast package management on Debian vs RHEL families.
notes.back: Debian/Ubuntu: apt/dpkg with .deb. RHEL/Fedora: dnf (or yum)/rpm with .rpm. e.g. apt install nginx vs dnf install nginx.

notes.front: What are SELinux modes and how do you toggle?
notes.back: Security-Enhanced Linux modes: enforcing (block + log), permissive (log only), disabled. getenforce/setenforce 0|1; persistent in /etc/selinux/config. Denials show in audit log; ausearch/chcon/restorecon manage contexts.

notes.front: How do you create a user with a home dir and set a password?
notes.back: useradd -m -s /bin/bash alice then passwd alice. Add to a group: usermod -aG sudo alice (the -a appends — omitting it replaces group membership). Users in /etc/passwd, groups in /etc/group.

notes.front: What does redirection and piping look like in bash?
notes.back: > overwrite stdout to file, >> append, 2> stderr, &> both, | pipe stdout to next command's stdin, < read stdin from file. e.g. cmd 2>&1 | tee log.

notes.front: What do grep, sed, and awk each do?
notes.back: grep: search lines by pattern (grep -r 'err' .). sed: stream-edit (sed 's/old/new/g'). awk: field-based processing (awk '{print $2}'). Core text-processing trio.
notes.source: Linux Foundation Certified SysAdmin · text tools

notes.front: How do you set up passwordless SSH key auth?
notes.back: ssh-keygen to make a keypair, then ssh-copy-id user@host (appends the public key to the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys). Private key stays local with 600 perms. Config in ~/.ssh/config.

notes.front: What is the difference between hard and soft (symbolic) links?
notes.back: A hard link is another name pointing to the same inode (same data; can't cross filesystems or link dirs). A symlink (ln -s) is a pointer to a path (can cross filesystems, can dangle if target removed).

notes.front: How do you check disk usage and free space?
notes.back: df -h shows filesystem free/used space; du -sh <dir> sums a directory's size; du -h --max-depth=1 breaks down children. lsblk shows block devices; ncdu is an interactive explorer.

notes.front: What does the default umask control?
notes.back: The permission bits masked off when creating files/dirs. umask 022 → new files 644, new dirs 755 (files never get execute by default). Subtract the mask from base perms (666 files / 777 dirs).

notes.front: How do you configure a basic firewall with firewalld or ufw?
notes.back: firewalld: firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent then --reload; zones group rules. ufw (Ubuntu): ufw allow 22/tcp, ufw enable. Both front-end nftables/iptables.

notes.front: What is the boot target system in systemd (vs runlevels)?
notes.back: systemd targets replace SysV runlevels: multi-user.target (≈ runlevel 3, no GUI), graphical.target (≈ 5). Set default with systemctl set-default multi-user.target; switch now with systemctl isolate.

notes.front: How do you archive and compress files with tar?
notes.back: tar -czf out.tar.gz dir/ create gzip archive; -xzf extract; -tzf list. Flags: c=create, x=extract, t=list, z=gzip, j=bzip2, f=file, v=verbose.

notes.front: What are the four Prometheus metric types?
notes.back: Counter (monotonically increasing, e.g. requests_total), Gauge (up/down, e.g. memory), Histogram (bucketed observations + _sum/_count), Summary (client-side quantiles + _sum/_count). Use rate() on counters and histograms.

notes.front: What does Prometheus's pull model do?
notes.back: Prometheus scrapes targets' HTTP /metrics endpoints on an interval (it pulls; targets don't push). Short-lived jobs use the Pushgateway as an exception. Pull simplifies target health detection and central config.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus time series uniquely identified by?
notes.back: The metric name plus the full set of label key/value pairs. Adding a label value creates a new series, so high-cardinality labels (user IDs, request IDs) explode memory — avoid them.

notes.front: What is the difference between rate() and irate()?
notes.back: Both compute per-second rate of a counter over a range. rate() averages across the whole window (smooth, good for alerts/dashboards). irate() uses only the last two samples (fast-reacting, spiky). Use rate() for slow alerting.

notes.front: How do you compute a 95th-percentile latency from a histogram?
notes.back: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))). The histogram exposes cumulative _bucket series labeled by le (less-or-equal upper bound); the quantile is interpolated server-side.

notes.front: What is the role of an exporter, and name a common one?
notes.back: An exporter exposes metrics from a system that doesn't speak Prometheus natively, in the text exposition format. node_exporter exposes host CPU/memory/disk/network. Others: blackbox_exporter (probing), kube-state-metrics (K8s object state).

notes.front: What is service discovery in Prometheus for?
notes.back: Dynamically finding scrape targets instead of hardcoding them — e.g. kubernetes_sd_configs discovers pods/services/nodes; relabeling rules filter/rewrite which are scraped and their labels. Essential in dynamic clusters.

notes.front: What is a recording rule and why use it?
notes.back: A precomputed expression saved as a new time series on each evaluation (record: in a rule group). Speeds up expensive/frequently-used queries and dashboards, and stabilizes alert expressions.

notes.front: How does an alerting rule's for clause work?
notes.back: An alerting rule fires when its expression is true; for: 5m requires the condition to hold continuously for that duration before transitioning from pending to firing, reducing flapping. Alerts are then sent to Alertmanager.

notes.front: What does Alertmanager do (grouping, inhibition, silencing)?
notes.back: Receives alerts from Prometheus and handles routing to receivers. Grouping batches related alerts into one notification; inhibition suppresses alerts when a higher-level one is firing; silencing mutes alerts matching labels for a window.

notes.front: What is the Pushgateway and its caveat?
notes.back: An intermediary that short-lived/batch jobs push metrics to, which Prometheus then scrapes. Caveat: it does not respect job lifecycle — stale pushed metrics persist until deleted, and it's not for long-running services.

notes.front: What is the difference between instant and range vectors?
notes.back: An instant vector is a set of series with a single value at one timestamp; a range vector selects values over a time window (e.g. metric[5m]). Functions like rate() require a range vector and return an instant vector.

notes.front: How does Prometheus store data (TSDB basics)?
notes.back: A local time-series database appending samples to in-memory blocks then flushing to disk blocks; a write-ahead log protects against crashes. It's intended for reliability over long-term clustering — remote_write/long-term backends (Thanos, Mimir, Cortex) extend retention/HA.

notes.front: What is the basic anatomy of a scrape_config?
notes.back: Defines a job_name, scrape interval/timeout, scheme, metrics path, and how to find targets (static_configs or *_sd_configs) plus relabel_configs. Each job tags its series with a job label.

notes.front: How do counters handle resets and why does rate() matter?
notes.back: Counters reset to 0 on process restart. rate()/increase() detect resets and correct for them, so you should never query a raw counter's difference manually — always wrap counters in rate()/increase().

notes.front: What is the USE and RED method for choosing metrics?
notes.back: USE (resources): Utilization, Saturation, Errors. RED (request-driven services): Rate, Errors, Duration. Frameworks for deciding which signals to alert/dashboard on.

notes.front: What are the Istio control-plane and data-plane components?
notes.back: Control plane: istiod (service discovery, config, certificate authority). Data plane: Envoy proxies — either sidecars (one per pod) or, in ambient mode, the ztunnel + waypoints. istiod pushes config to proxies via xDS.

notes.front: What does an Istio VirtualService configure?
notes.back: L7 routing rules for a host: match on URI/headers/weights and route to subsets/destinations. Enables traffic splitting (canary), header-based routing, retries, timeouts, and fault injection. Paired with a DestinationRule.

notes.front: What does a DestinationRule define?
notes.back: Policies applied after routing to a destination: named subsets (by pod labels, e.g. v1/v2), load-balancing algorithm, connection pool limits, and outlier detection (circuit breaking). VirtualService routes to subsets defined here.

notes.front: How do you do a canary/weighted release in Istio?
notes.back: In a VirtualService, route with weights across subsets: e.g. 90% to subset v1, 10% to subset v2 (subsets defined in a DestinationRule). Shift weights gradually to ramp the new version.

notes.front: What is the Istio Gateway resource?
notes.back: Configures a load balancer at the mesh edge for inbound (or outbound) traffic — which ports/protocols/hosts are exposed. A VirtualService then binds to the Gateway to route that ingress traffic to mesh services.

notes.front: What does a ServiceEntry do?
notes.back: Adds an external service into Istio's service registry so mesh workloads can route to it with Istio policies (and apply mTLS/telemetry to egress). Used to reach external APIs/databases under mesh control.

notes.front: What does PeerAuthentication control and what are its modes?
notes.back: Sets mutual-TLS requirements for traffic received by workloads. Modes: STRICT (only mTLS), PERMISSIVE (mTLS or plaintext — default, eases migration), DISABLE. Scope: mesh-wide, namespace, or workload.

notes.front: What is RequestAuthentication vs AuthorizationPolicy?
notes.back: RequestAuthentication validates end-user credentials (JWT issuer/JWKS) — it authenticates but doesn't authorize. AuthorizationPolicy then ALLOW/DENY/CUSTOM based on source identity, namespace, JWT claims, methods, paths.

notes.front: How does Istio establish workload identity for mTLS?
notes.back: istiod acts as a CA issuing X.509 certs to each workload, with identity encoded as a SPIFFE ID (spiffe://<trust-domain>/ns/<ns>/sa/<serviceaccount>) derived from the pod's ServiceAccount. mTLS authenticates both ends by this identity.

notes.front: What is fault injection in Istio used for?
notes.back: Deliberately injecting delays or aborts (e.g. return HTTP 500 to 10% of requests) via a VirtualService, to test application resilience and failure handling without changing app code.

notes.front: What is outlier detection (circuit breaking) in Istio?
notes.back: In a DestinationRule, automatically eject backend endpoints that return consecutive errors from the load-balancing pool for a cooldown, preventing a failing instance from dragging down the service. Combined with connection-pool limits.

notes.front: Sidecar mode vs ambient mode in Istio?
notes.back: Sidecar: an Envoy proxy injected into every pod (full L7, higher per-pod overhead). Ambient (GA in Istio 1.24): no sidecars — a per-node ztunnel handles L4 mTLS, and optional waypoint proxies add L7 only where needed, reducing overhead.

notes.front: What is ztunnel and HBONE in Istio ambient mode?
notes.back: ztunnel (zero-trust tunnel) is a per-node Rust proxy (DaemonSet) doing L4 mTLS, auth, and telemetry. HBONE (HTTP-Based Overlay Network Environment) is the HTTP CONNECT-based, mTLS-encrypted tunneling protocol (port 15008) carrying traffic between ztunnels/waypoints.

notes.front: What is a waypoint proxy and how is it deployed?
notes.back: An Envoy proxy providing L7 features (HTTP routing, retries, L7 authz) in ambient mode, shared per namespace/service-account rather than per pod. Deployed via the Kubernetes Gateway API with gatewayClassName: istio-waypoint (e.g. istioctl waypoint apply).

notes.front: What does istioctl analyze / proxy-config help with?
notes.back: istioctl analyze validates config for problems before/after apply. istioctl proxy-config <cluster|route|listener|endpoint> <pod> dumps the Envoy config a sidecar received — the primary way to debug why traffic isn't routing as expected.

notes.front: What telemetry does Istio provide out of the box?
notes.back: Proxies emit standardized L7 metrics (request count, duration, size), access logs, and distributed-trace spans, plus service-graph data — without app changes. Integrates with Prometheus/Grafana/Jaeger/Kiali.

notes.front: What is eBPF and why does Cilium use it?
notes.back: extended Berkeley Packet Filter runs sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel on hooks (sockets, XDP, tc) without changing kernel source. Cilium uses it for high-performance networking, security, and observability — enforcing policy in-kernel and replacing iptables-based dataplanes.

notes.front: How does Cilium's identity-based security differ from IP-based?
notes.back: Cilium assigns a security identity derived from pod labels, not IP addresses. Policy is enforced on identity, so it remains correct as pods churn and IPs are reused — more scalable than IP/CIDR rules in dynamic clusters.

notes.front: What does a CiliumNetworkPolicy add over the standard NetworkPolicy?
notes.back: The standard NetworkPolicy is L3/L4 only. CiliumNetworkPolicy adds L7 awareness — e.g. allow only HTTP GET /api, specific Kafka topics, or DNS-name-based egress (toFQDNs) — plus cluster-wide policies.

notes.front: What is Hubble?
notes.back: Cilium's observability layer built on eBPF: provides flow-level visibility (which identity talked to which, allowed/denied, L7 verbs), a service map, and metrics — without app instrumentation. CLI (hubble observe) and a UI.

notes.front: What does "kube-proxy replacement" mean in Cilium?
notes.back: Cilium implements Service load balancing (ClusterIP, NodePort, etc.) directly in eBPF, removing the need for kube-proxy and its iptables rules. This improves performance and scalability, especially at high Service counts.

notes.front: What is Cluster Mesh in Cilium?
notes.back: Connects multiple Kubernetes clusters into a single network/identity domain — enabling cross-cluster service discovery, load balancing, and network policy, with global services and failover across clusters.

notes.front: What transparent encryption options does Cilium offer?
notes.back: In-cluster traffic encryption via WireGuard (simple, fast) or IPsec, configured at the agent level — no app changes. Encrypts node-to-node pod traffic for data-in-transit compliance.

notes.front: What is a Cilium Endpoint and Identity?
notes.back: An Endpoint represents a managed networked entity (usually a pod) on a node. Its Identity is the numeric security identity derived from its labels; policy and Hubble flows reference identities. Inspect with cilium endpoint list.

notes.front: What is Tetragon?
notes.back: A Cilium-project eBPF-based runtime security observability + enforcement tool: tracks process execution, file/network access, and can enforce/kill on policy violations at the kernel level — complementary to Falco-style detection.

notes.front: How does Cilium support egress to external services by DNS name?
notes.back: With toFQDNs rules in a CiliumNetworkPolicy, Cilium intercepts DNS, learns the resolved IPs, and allows egress only to those FQDNs — solving the problem that external IPs are dynamic and not known in advance.

notes.front: What is XDP and where does it run?
notes.back: eXpress Data Path is the earliest eBPF networking hook, at the NIC driver level before the kernel network stack — used for very high-performance packet processing/filtering (e.g. DDoS drop, load balancing) in Cilium.

notes.front: What are the default-deny semantics once a CiliumNetworkPolicy selects a pod?
notes.back: As with standard policy, the moment any policy selects an endpoint for a direction (ingress/egress), that direction switches to default-deny for that endpoint, and only explicitly allowed flows pass. Unselected endpoints stay default-allow.

notes.front: What does the Cilium agent do on each node?
notes.back: Runs as a DaemonSet, manages eBPF programs/maps, assigns identities, enforces policy, programs Service load balancing, and reports to Hubble. The operator handles cluster-wide tasks (IPAM, CRD GC).

notes.front: How does Cilium relate to the Gateway API and Ingress?
notes.back: Cilium can act as a Gateway API / Ingress controller itself (eBPF-based L7 routing), consolidating CNI + load balancing + ingress in one dataplane rather than running a separate ingress controller.

notes.front: What are the four OpenGitOps principles?
notes.back: GitOps systems are: 1) Declarative (desired state expressed declaratively); 2) Versioned and immutable (stored in Git, full history); 3) Pulled automatically (agents pull approved state); 4) Continuously reconciled (controllers detect drift and converge actual→desired).

notes.front: Push-based vs pull-based deployment, and which is GitOps-native?
notes.back: Push: a CI pipeline runs kubectl apply into the cluster (credentials live in CI). Pull: an in-cluster agent (Argo CD/Flux) watches Git and applies changes itself. Pull is GitOps-native — better security (no external cluster creds) and continuous reconciliation.

notes.front: What is drift and how does GitOps handle it?
notes.back: Drift is divergence between the live cluster and the Git-declared desired state (e.g. a manual kubectl edit). A GitOps reconciler detects it and either reports or auto-corrects (self-heal), restoring Git as the source of truth.

notes.front: What is the difference between the desired state and the observed/actual state?
notes.back: Desired state = what Git declares should exist. Actual/observed state = what's running in the cluster. The reconciliation loop continuously drives actual toward desired; the difference is the drift to be resolved.

notes.front: Why is Git the source of truth advantageous for operations?
notes.back: Every change is a reviewed, versioned, auditable commit; rollback is git revert; access control uses existing Git/PR workflows; and recovery/rebuild is reproducible from the repo. Improves auditability, security, and disaster recovery.

notes.front: What is the role of an environment/config repo separation?
notes.back: Common pattern: app source repo (code) is separate from a config/deployment repo (manifests). CI builds and updates an image tag in the config repo; the GitOps agent deploys from the config repo. Keeps deploy state declarative and decoupled from app builds.

notes.front: What does "reconciliation is continuous, not one-shot" mean?
notes.back: The agent re-checks desired vs actual on an ongoing loop (not just at deploy time), so out-of-band changes are continuously corrected and the system self-heals — distinct from a one-time apply in a classic pipeline.

notes.front: How does GitOps relate to but differ from CI/CD?
notes.back: CI builds/tests artifacts; CD delivers them. GitOps is a specific way to do the CD/deploy half: declarative, Git-driven, pull-based, continuously reconciled. CI still runs outside the cluster; GitOps governs what lands in it.

notes.front: What are common GitOps tools?
notes.back: Argo CD and Flux (both CNCF graduated) are the dominant reconciler agents. Supporting tools: Kustomize/Helm for templating, Kargo for promotion, sealed-secrets/External Secrets for secret handling in Git.

notes.front: What is a key challenge GitOps must solve around secrets?
notes.back: Plaintext secrets must never sit in Git. Solutions: encrypt before commit (Sealed Secrets, SOPS) or keep secrets external and reference them (External Secrets Operator pulling from Vault/cloud KMS). The reconciler handles the encrypted/reference form.

notes.front: What problem does Backstage solve?
notes.back: An open-source framework (originated at Spotify, CNCF) for building an Internal Developer Portal (IDP): a single pane unifying the software catalog, docs, scaffolding, and tooling — reducing developer cognitive load and standardizing how services are created and discovered.

notes.front: What are the core entity kinds in the Backstage Software Catalog?
notes.back: Component (a thing you build/run), API (an interface a component exposes/consumes), Resource (infrastructure dependency), System (group of components), Domain (group of systems), Group/User (org/ownership), Template (scaffolder), Location (points at entity descriptors).

notes.front: What is the catalog-info.yaml file?
notes.back: The descriptor (usually in each repo) registering an entity in the catalog — e.g. kind: Component with metadata (name, annotations) and spec (type, lifecycle, owner). Backstage ingests it via a Location to populate the catalog.

notes.front: What is the Scaffolder / Software Templates feature?
notes.back: Backstage's golden-path creation tool. A kind: Template defines parameters (a form the developer fills) and ordered steps (actions like fetch:template, publish:github, catalog:register) that generate a new repo/service and register it — standardizing how new software starts.

notes.front: What is TechDocs?
notes.back: Backstage's docs-as-code feature: Markdown docs (typically MkDocs) live next to code and render in the portal on the entity's page, discovered via the backstage.io/techdocs-ref annotation. Keeps documentation versioned with the service.

notes.front: How is Backstage extended?
notes.back: Through plugins (frontend + backend). The catalog, scaffolder, TechDocs, and search are themselves plugins. A rich plugin ecosystem integrates CI/CD, cloud, monitoring, and security tools into entity pages. Backstage is a framework you build your own portal from.

notes.front: What is the ownership model in the catalog?
notes.back: Every entity has a spec.owner referencing a Group (preferred) or User — the team responsible. Drives accountability, notifications, and filtering. A common scorecard rule: every Component must be owned by a Group, not a User.

notes.front: How does Backstage discover and keep the catalog up to date?
notes.back: Processors/providers ingest entities from registered Locations (Git repos, URLs) or auto-discovery rules, then periodically re-read them. The materialized entity graph is stored (PostgreSQL in production); search indexes catalog + TechDocs.

notes.front: What is the relationship between System, Component, and API entities?
notes.back: A System groups related Components that work together; Components can providesApis/consumesApis referencing API entities; multiple Systems roll up into a Domain. This models architecture and dependencies for discovery.

notes.front: Why does Backstage matter for platform engineering?
notes.back: It's the typical UI of an Internal Developer Platform — exposing self-service golden paths (templates), discoverability (catalog), and docs in one place, so the platform is consumed as a product. CNPA explicitly references it as the portal layer.

notes.front: What are the signals OpenTelemetry covers?
notes.back: Traces, Metrics, and Logs (the three core signals), plus emerging support for profiles and the cross-cutting baggage. OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the CNCF standard for generating/collecting/exporting telemetry, vendor-neutral.

notes.front: What is a span and a trace?
notes.back: A span is a single timed operation (name, start/end, attributes, status, events). A trace is a tree of spans sharing a trace ID, representing one request's path across services. Parent/child links via span IDs build the tree.

notes.front: What is context propagation in OpenTelemetry?
notes.back: Passing trace context (trace ID, span ID, flags) across service boundaries so spans link into one trace. Uses the W3C traceparent/tracestate HTTP headers. Baggage propagates arbitrary user-defined key/values alongside it.

notes.front: What is the OpenTelemetry Collector and its pipeline stages?
notes.back: A vendor-agnostic agent/gateway that ingests, processes, and exports telemetry. Pipeline = receivers (intake, e.g. OTLP) → processors (batch, filter, transform) → exporters (send to backends). Decouples apps from observability backends.

notes.front: What is OTLP?
notes.back: The OpenTelemetry Protocol — the native wire protocol (gRPC or HTTP, protobuf) for transmitting traces/metrics/logs between SDKs, Collectors, and backends. The default, standardized export format.

notes.front: Auto-instrumentation vs manual instrumentation?
notes.back: Auto: agents/libraries instrument common frameworks with no code changes (fast coverage). Manual: you call the OTel API/SDK to create custom spans/metrics for business logic. Typically combine both.

notes.front: What is the difference between the OTel API and SDK?
notes.back: The API defines instrumentation interfaces apps/libraries code against (no-op if unconfigured). The SDK is the implementation that actually samples, processes, and exports. Libraries depend only on the API; the app wires in the SDK.

notes.front: What are semantic conventions?
notes.back: Standardized names for attributes and metrics (e.g. http.request.method, service.name) so telemetry is consistent and portable across languages/vendors/backends. Without them, dashboards/queries can't be reused.

notes.front: Head sampling vs tail sampling?
notes.back: Head: the sampling decision is made at trace start (cheap, but blind to outcome). Tail: decide after the full trace is seen (e.g. keep all errors/slow traces) — done in the Collector, more useful but needs buffering.

notes.front: What is a Resource in OpenTelemetry?
notes.back: Immutable attributes describing the entity producing telemetry (e.g. service.name, service.version, host, k8s pod). Attached to all signals so a backend can attribute data to the right service/instance.

notes.front: What is an exemplar in metrics?
notes.back: A sample data point on a metric (e.g. a histogram bucket) that carries a trace ID, linking an aggregate metric back to a specific representative trace — bridging metrics and traces for drill-down.

notes.front: What were OpenTracing and OpenCensus relative to OpenTelemetry?
notes.back: Two earlier projects that merged to form OpenTelemetry — OpenTracing (tracing API) + OpenCensus (metrics + tracing libs). OTel is the converged, CNCF-hosted standard superseding both.

notes.front: Why deploy the Collector as both agent and gateway?
notes.back: Agent (per node/sidecar) collects locally with low latency; gateway (central pool) does heavier processing (tail sampling, batching) and fans out to backends. Separating them scales and centralizes export config.

notes.front: What span status and span kinds exist?
notes.back: Status: Unset, Ok, Error. Kinds: SERVER, CLIENT, PRODUCER, CONSUMER, INTERNAL — describing the span's role in a request, which helps backends render service topology correctly.

notes.front: What is Kyverno and how does it differ from OPA/Gatekeeper?
notes.back: A Kubernetes-native policy engine that runs as an admission controller (validating + mutating webhooks). Policies are plain YAML — no Rego to learn (unlike OPA Gatekeeper). It can validate, mutate, generate, verify images, and clean up resources. CNCF incubating.

notes.front: What are Kyverno's rule types?
notes.back: Each rule does exactly one of: validate (allow/block), mutate (modify the resource), generate (create dependent resources), or verifyImages (check image signatures via Cosign/Sigstore). Cleanup is a separate CleanupPolicy type.

notes.front: Policy vs ClusterPolicy in Kyverno?
notes.back: Policy is namespaced (applies within one namespace); ClusterPolicy applies cluster-wide. Both contain a list of rules with match/exclude selectors and one action declaration each.

notes.front: What does validationFailureAction (failureAction) control?
notes.back: Whether a failed validate rule blocks the request (Enforce) or merely logs it to a policy report (Audit). Standard rollout: start in Audit to gauge impact, then switch to Enforce.

notes.front: What is background scanning in Kyverno?
notes.back: Periodic re-evaluation (default hourly) of existing resources against validate/verifyImages rules, recording results in PolicyReports/ClusterPolicyReports. It never blocks already-running resources even in Enforce mode — admission control handles new/changed ones.

notes.front: What are PolicyReports?
notes.back: Kubernetes custom resources Kyverno generates with per-resource results (pass, fail, warn, error, skip). They reflect current state (not history) and back tools like Policy Reporter. Namespaced = PolicyReport, cluster = ClusterPolicyReport.

notes.front: Give an example of a Kyverno generate rule use case.
notes.back: When a new Namespace is created, automatically generate a default-deny NetworkPolicy and a ResourceQuota in it — so governance defaults appear without manual steps. Generate can also keep generated resources in sync with their source.

notes.front: How does Kyverno verify image signatures?
notes.back: A verifyImages rule checks signatures/attestations (keyed or keyless) using Cosign/Sigstore; unsigned or untrusted images are rejected at admission. Enforces supply-chain provenance.

notes.front: What is a PolicyException?
notes.back: A resource that exempts specific resources/namespaces from named policy rules — a controlled escape hatch so you don't have to weaken the policy itself or sprinkle excludes everywhere. Can be scoped and governed.

notes.front: How do mutate and validate rules order during admission?
notes.back: All mutation rules across all policies apply first, then validation rules — so validation sees the already-mutated object. This lets a mutate rule add a default that a validate rule then confirms.

notes.front: How do you test Kyverno policies before applying?
notes.back: The Kyverno CLI: kyverno apply runs policies against manifests locally, and kyverno test runs declarative test cases (expected results) — slot into CI to catch regressions before cluster rollout.

notes.front: What are Kyverno's controllers in v3.x?
notes.back: Split into four independently scalable controllers: admission (webhook enforcement), background (scans existing resources, mutate-existing/generate), cleanup (CleanupPolicy/TTL deletion), and reports (PolicyReports).

notes.front: What is platform engineering, and how does it differ from DevOps?
notes.back: Building an Internal Developer Platform (IDP) as a product that gives developers self-service, paved-road access to infrastructure/tooling. DevOps is a culture/practice spreading ownership; platform engineering productizes the underlying capabilities so dev teams aren't each reinventing them.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · fundamentals

notes.front: What is a "golden path" / paved road?
notes.back: An opinionated, supported, well-documented default way to build and ship a service (templates + pipelines + guardrails). Optional but easiest — developers get speed and safety; the platform team gets consistency. A core CNPA concept.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · golden paths

notes.front: What does "treat the platform as a product" mean?
notes.back: Apply product thinking to the internal platform: real users (developers), discovery of their needs, a roadmap, UX, documentation, support, and adoption metrics — rather than a pile of tools imposed top-down. Adoption is voluntary, so it must be genuinely better.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · product mindset

notes.front: What is an Internal Developer Platform (IDP)?
notes.back: The self-service layer of capabilities (provisioning, CI/CD, environments, observability, security) that developers consume to ship software without filing tickets to ops. Often surfaced via a portal like Backstage. The "what you build" in platform engineering.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · IDP

notes.front: What does Team Topologies contribute to platform engineering?
notes.back: It defines the platform team as one of four fundamental team types, whose job is to reduce other teams' cognitive load by providing self-service capabilities "as a product," interacting via the X-as-a-Service mode.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · org design

notes.front: What are the DORA metrics?
notes.back: DevOps Research and Assessment delivery metrics: Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, and Time to Restore Service (MTTR). Used to measure delivery performance and a platform's impact.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · measurement

notes.front: What is the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model?
notes.back: A model assessing platform maturity across aspects (investment, adoption, interfaces, operations, measurement) at levels like Provisional → Operational → Scalable → Optimizing. Used to plan a platform's evolution rather than judging it as done.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · maturity

notes.front: What is Crossplane and why does it matter for platforms?
notes.back: A CNCF tool that turns infrastructure provisioning into Kubernetes APIs: define Composite Resources and Compositions so developers request infra (DBs, buckets) via simple CRDs while the platform controls the implementation. Enables self-service infra with guardrails.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · provisioning

notes.front: What is the "thinnest viable platform" idea?
notes.back: Start a platform as small as possible — even a wiki page documenting the paved road — and grow only where it removes real friction. Avoids over-building a heavyweight platform nobody adopts.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · approach

notes.front: Continuous Integration vs Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment?
notes.back: CI: merge + build + test frequently. Continuous Delivery: every passing build is releasable, deploy on a click. Continuous Deployment: every passing build auto-deploys to prod with no manual gate. Platforms standardize these pipelines.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · delivery

notes.front: What does "declarative resource management" mean for platforms?
notes.back: Express desired infra/app state declaratively (manifests/CRDs) and let controllers reconcile — the basis for GitOps, Operators, and Crossplane. Platforms favor declarative + reconciled over imperative scripts for reliability and auditability.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · declarative

notes.front: What does developer experience (DevEx) optimize for, and what's the enemy?
notes.back: Optimizes flow, fast feedback, and low friction to ship safely. The enemy is excessive cognitive load — forcing developers to understand the entire infra stack. Platforms abstract that away behind self-service interfaces.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · developer experience

notes.front: What does "secure by default" mean in a platform context?
notes.back: The paved road bakes in security (mTLS, scanned images, policy enforcement, least-privilege RBAC, network policy) so doing the easy thing is also the secure thing — developers get it without having to be security experts. CNPA exam phrasing cue.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · security

notes.front: What platform capabilities map to observability/conformance?
notes.back: Standardized metrics/logs/traces (OpenTelemetry, Prometheus), golden-signal dashboards, plus policy engines (Kyverno/OPA) and conformance checks that enforce org standards across all workloads automatically.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · observability

notes.front: How do you measure a platform's success beyond DORA?
notes.back: Track adoption (teams/services onboarded), developer satisfaction (surveys), self-service rate (tickets avoided), and time-to-first-deploy for new services — i.e. product KPIs proving the platform is reducing friction.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate · measurement

notes.front: What does the CNPE certification add over CNPA?
notes.back: Certified Cloud Native Platform Engineer is the performance-based, professional-level exam: you actually build/operate platform components (GitOps delivery, provisioning APIs, observability, security/policy) hands-on, vs CNPA's multiple-choice associate scope.

notes.front: In platform work, why prefer Operators/controllers for day-2 automation?
notes.back: They encode operational logic to continuously reconcile complex stateful systems (DBs, certs, backups) — turning manual runbooks into self-healing automation exposed as CRDs, which is the self-service primitive a platform builds on.

notes.front: What is a sensible promotion strategy across environments in a platform?
notes.back: Promote the same immutable artifact (image digest) dev→staging→prod via Git changes (GitOps), gated by automated tests/policy and progressive delivery (canary/blue-green). Tools like Kargo orchestrate promotion across stages.

notes.front: How should a platform expose infrastructure provisioning safely?
notes.back: Via abstracted self-service APIs (Crossplane composites, Operators, or templates) that encapsulate sane defaults, policy, cost and security guardrails — developers request a "database" not raw cloud primitives, and the platform controls the how.

notes.front: What progressive delivery techniques should a platform support?
notes.back: Canary (shift a small % of traffic, watch metrics, ramp), blue-green (full standby, instant switch), and automated analysis/rollback on SLO breach (e.g. Argo Rollouts + metrics). Reduces blast radius of releases.
notes.source: Cloud Native Platform Engineer · progressive delivery

notes.front: What is Argo CD and its core object?
notes.back: A GitOps continuous-delivery controller for Kubernetes. Its core object is the Application: it points at a Git repo/path (source) and a destination cluster/namespace, and continuously reconciles the cluster to match Git. CNCF graduated.
notes.source: Certified Argo Project Associate · Argo CD

notes.front: What do Argo CD sync status and health status mean?
notes.back: Sync status: is the live state in sync with Git (Synced vs OutOfSync/drift)? Health status: are the resources actually healthy (Healthy, Progressing, Degraded)? They're orthogonal — synced doesn't guarantee healthy.
notes.source: Certified Argo Project Associate · Argo CD

notes.front: What is the "app of apps" pattern in Argo CD?
notes.back: A parent Application whose Git source contains child Application manifests — letting you bootstrap and manage many apps declaratively from one root. ApplicationSets are the more dynamic, templated successor for generating apps.
notes.source: Certified Argo Project Associate · Argo CD

notes.front: What are Argo CD sync waves and hooks?
notes.back: Sync waves (argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave annotation) order resource application (low→high). Hooks (PreSync/Sync/PostSync) run jobs at phases — e.g. a PreSync DB migration before the app rolls out.
notes.source: Certified Argo Project Associate · Argo CD

notes.front: What does auto-sync with self-heal and prune do in Argo CD?
notes.back: Auto-sync applies Git changes automatically. Self-heal reverts live drift back to Git. Prune deletes resources removed from Git. Together they make the cluster strictly track the repo.
notes.source: Certified Argo Project Associate · Argo CD

notes.front: What is Argo Workflows?
notes.back: A Kubernetes-native workflow engine where each step runs in a container, orchestrated as a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) or sequential steps. Used for CI, batch/data pipelines, and ML jobs. Each Workflow is a CRD.

notes.front: What is the difference between steps and dag templates in Argo Workflows?
notes.back: steps: a list of sequential stages (items within a stage run in parallel). dag: tasks declare dependencies, and the engine runs them as soon as their deps complete — more flexible parallelism.

notes.front: What is Argo Rollouts?
notes.back: A controller replacing the standard Deployment with advanced strategies: canary and blue-green, with traffic shaping (via ingress/mesh) and automated analysis that promotes or aborts based on metrics. Enables progressive delivery.

notes.front: What is an AnalysisTemplate in Argo Rollouts?
notes.back: Defines metric queries (Prometheus, etc.) and success/failure conditions evaluated during a canary step. If metrics breach thresholds, the rollout automatically pauses/aborts and rolls back — automated quality gating of releases.

notes.front: What is Argo Events?
notes.back: An event-driven automation framework: EventSources ingest events (webhooks, queues, cron), Sensors evaluate dependencies and trigger actions (e.g. start an Argo Workflow). Connects external events to in-cluster automation.

notes.front: What is an Argo CD Project (AppProject)?
notes.back: A grouping that constrains Applications: which source repos, destination clusters/namespaces, and resource kinds are allowed, plus RBAC. Provides multi-tenancy guardrails so teams can't deploy outside their boundary.
notes.source: Certified Argo Project Associate · Argo CD

notes.front: How does Argo CD handle blue-green vs canary at the deployment object level?
notes.back: Argo CD itself just syncs manifests; progressive delivery is done by Argo Rollouts via its Rollout CRD (canary/blue-green steps). Argo CD deploys the Rollout object; Rollouts executes the strategy.

notes.front: What multi-container pod patterns should you know (CKAD/CKA gap)?
notes.back: Sidecar (helper alongside main, e.g. log shipper — now a native initContainer with restartPolicy: Always), ambassador (proxy to outside world), adapter (normalize output). Containers in a pod share network + volumes.

notes.front: What are the three probe types and their effects?
notes.back: liveness (restart container if failing), readiness (remove pod from Service endpoints until passing), startup (gate the other probes for slow-starting apps). Each can be httpGet/tcpSocket/exec/grpc.

notes.front: What is Kustomize and how does it differ from Helm?
notes.back: A template-free customization tool (built into kubectl: kubectl apply -k). A base + overlays patch manifests per environment — no templating language. Helm uses Go templates + packaging/releases; Kustomize is pure YAML overlays.

notes.front: What deployment strategies does the built-in Deployment support?
notes.back: RollingUpdate (default; maxSurge/maxUnavailable control pace) and Recreate (kill all then start new — brief downtime). Canary/blue-green need extra tooling (Argo Rollouts/mesh).

notes.front: What is the difference between a Job and a CronJob?
notes.back: A Job runs pods to completion (with completions/parallelism and backoffLimit). A CronJob creates Jobs on a cron schedule. Use for batch/one-off tasks rather than long-running services.
